transport: RS-485 to WiFi / Bluetooth transparent serial server. RJ45 to the controller or inverter, directly powered from the RS485 port's 5 VDC. Port baud rate 300 bps–230400 bps, default 115200. Range ≤ 50 m (eBox-WIFI-01) / ≤ 20 m (WiFi 2.4G RJ45 D). What the datasheet does NOT state: the TCP port number, and whether the LAN side speaks Modbus TCP or a raw socket carrying Modbus RTU frames. Both null.

refutedOnReview: Fully refuted. The five committed PDFs exist and the eBox-WIFI-01 "Applicable Models" table is quoted accurately (LS-B, VS-A, VS-BN, Tracer-A, Tracer-BN, SHI, STI on RJ45; eTracer-AD, eTracer-BND, iTracer-ND on 3.81-4P; port baud 300bps~230400bps default 115200; RS485-to-WiFi), but nothing supports a shared register map. gotchas: A bridge, not a device. It changes the transport under an existing dialect; it does not have a register map, a DeviceKind, or any metric of its own. Filed under lan-http because that is where the transport lands, but the register map on the far side is still epever-tracer-a or epever-inverter-v1.

The one genuinely useful consequence: it removes the RS-485 cable run without changing the driver, IF the LAN side turns out to be plain Modbus TCP. The datasheet does not say that it is. Until someone puts a packet capture on it, treat "just point the Modbus TCP client at it" as unverified.

eBox-BLE-01 is Bluetooth and is designed around EPEver's phone app rather than a generic client. Nothing read here documents a BLE GATT service or characteristic, so it is a dead end for a driver until a vendor document surfaces.

The bridge occupies the controller's single RJ45 port. It cannot coexist with an MT50 on the same socket, and putting both on the bus reintroduces the two-masters collision noted under epever-tracer-a.

The RS485-1M2S extension module (one master, two slaves) is the vendor's own answer to that problem and has its own datasheet at epever.com/upload/file/2109/EPEVER-Datasheet-RS485-1M2S.pdf. Not examined in this sweep.
